content_list.content_text: Michael Curtiz's (1886-1962) Yankee Doodle Dandy (1942) was in tune with the mood of a nation entering World War II, being patriotic, sentimental, aggressive and almost a deification of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, as were its pretentious subject and the songs and choreography of George M. Cohan (James Cagney). The closing of markets in war-ravaged Europe forced Hollywood to seek foreign income in Latin America, which led to a mini boom of Latin American musicals such as Down Argentine Way (1940), starring Carmen Miranda (1909-1955).

information.contentTitle: Trailer for Down Argentine Way (1940) with Carmen Miranda
information.contentText: Featuring Betty Grable in her first major film role, Down Argentine Way includes a special appearance by Carmen Miranda in her first American film.

content_list.content_text: The general tone was one of exaggerated cheer in the star-studded cast of Thank Your Lucky Stars (1943). By contrast, Meet Me in St. Louis (1944), by Vincente Minnelli (1903-1986) and starring Judy Garland (1922-1969), was a nostalgic, bittersweet film that revolved around old songs, looking back to the turn of the 20th century.

After the war, biopics of singers such as Al Jolson (Larry Parks) in The Jolson Story (1946), or of composers such as Cole Porter (Cary Grant) in Night and Day (1946), continued to prevail. Heavily fictionalized and artificial, this cycle relied on time-honored clichés.

Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers, the great musical stars of the 1930s, reunited for one last, weak film, The Barkleys of Broadway (1949), but Astaire was much more at ease in the company of singer Bing Crosby in films such as Holiday Inn (1942). His standing as the leading name in musicals was being threatened by the younger and obviously more athletic Gene Kelly (1912-1996), who debuted with For Me and My Gal (1942) and was soon creating innovative works such as Anchors Aweigh (1945), in which he dances with the cartoon star MGM's Jerry Mouse, and Cover Girl (1944), in which he dances with his own reflection.

information.contentTitle: Como Gene Kelly dançou com o rato Jerry em Marujos do Amor (1945)
information.contentText: Originally, Mickey Mouse was to be the cartoon character in the famous musical scene with Gene Kelly. However, since Walt Disney refused to authorize the use of the character in a film produced by MGM, Kelly decided to use a character from the animation studio of MGM Studios itself: Jerry the mouse, of Tom and Jerry.

content_list.content_text: Anchors Aweigh, about sailors on leave desperate to see a show at the Hollywood Bowl, and the sports-themed Take Me Out to the Ball Game (1949), the last film directed solely by Busby Berkeley (1895-1976), are forerunners of On the Town (1949). Directed by Gene Kelly and Stanley Donen (b. 1924) and inspired by Leonard Bernstein's 1944 Broadway show, the songwriting team of Bernstein, Adolph Green and Betty Comden worked with Roger Edens on several numbers for the film.

content_list.title: Hollywood on Hollywood
content_list.description: Cinema has been filming itself since the silent era (Merton of the Movies, 1924). A devastating mix of gossip, glamour, tragedy and a touch of self-promotion makes up the similar What Price Hollywood? (1932) and A Star Is Born (1937, 1954, 1976 and 2018). A later cycle deals with sacred monsters in gothic California mansions, starting with the pessimistic Sunset Boulevard (1950). Specific segments of the film industry are examined in Ed Wood (1994) and Gods and Monsters (1998). But Michael Powell's (1905-1990) Peeping Tom (1960), about a cameraman and killer, and Richard Rush's (b. 1929) The Stunt Man (1980), featuring a Mephistophelean director, suggest that there is something sick about the art of filmmaking.

content_list.content_text: In its dazzling opening number, shot outside the studio, the film escapes the stage artificiality seen in all previous musicals, even though some of its best moments are as fanciful, staged and stylized as those of any Minnelli film. Throughout the decade, Minnelli, Donen-Kelly and Astaire waged a creative battle, making musicals evolve in leaps and elegant spins.

quote.quote: Gene wasn't afraid of competition. If you could be better than he was, he loved it
quote.author: Donald O'Connor on Singin' in the Rain

content_list.content_text: Kelly worked with Minnelli on the Oscar-winning An American in Paris (1951), which revolved around the repertoire of George Gershwin, but returned to work with Donen on Singin' in the Rain (1952). Both films were highly praised and became huge hits. But there is a slight difference between Minnelli's somewhat pretentious work and Donen's, which was simpler and poked fun at itself.

information.contentText: The film became historic as the first musical to be shot on location. Gene Kelly insisted that some scenes be shot in New York rather than in a studio, as was common at the time. They were filmed at the American Museum of Natural History, on the Brooklyn Bridge and at Rockefeller Center.

content_list.content_text: For example, the motto of Kelly's vain movie star is "Dignity, always dignity", inspired by the tumbling of his vaudeville shows early in his career. Interestingly, this became the theme of Minnelli's answer film, the innovative, risqué and divinely creative backstage musical The Band Wagon (1953). Astaire, whose contribution to artificial choreography had been the dance on the ceiling in Royal Wedding (1951), plays musical star Tony Hunter, who hears jokes about his age for much of the film and is paired with a ballerina played by Cyd Charisse, in the first of her spectacular performances.

Without Kelly, Donen directed Seven Brides for Seven Brothers (1954), a Western musical shot outdoors and conceived for the screen, starring the virile baritone Howard Keel, with an emphasis on Michael Kidd's lively choreography. With Kelly, Donen made It's Always Fair Weather (1955), a disillusioned, though interesting, follow-up to On the Town.

information.contentText: After watching Dorothy Dandridge's screen test, Preminger declared it was the best he had ever seen.

content_list.content_text: The Broadway hit Oklahoma! (1943) was the emblematic musical of its time, but it only reached the screen in 1955. Directed by Fred Zinnemann (1907-1997), its long run encouraged Western musicals off the singing-cowboy trail, but its importance lies in confirming the direct link between Broadway and Hollywood, which kept up a flow of stage-to-screen adaptations throughout the decade, among them Show Boat (1951), Carmen Jones (1954), Guys and Dolls (1955), The King and I (1956), South Pacific (1958) and Porgy and Bess (1959).

Some of them allowed film and music stars such as Doris Day and Sinatra to take on celebrated roles with great songs; others allowed stage actors such as Yul Brynner to repeat the great performances of their careers; and still others surprisingly cast Rossano Brazzi as a French aristocrat, or Marlon Brando, who was no singer, as the lead in musicals.

information.contentTitle: Marlon Brando - Luck Be a Lady in Guys and Dolls (1955)
information.contentText: The audio for each of Marlon Brando's musical numbers was pieced together from several recordings.

content_list.content_text: The 1950s created old-fashioned showcases for talents such as Marilyn Monroe (1926-1962) and Jane Russell in Howard Hawks's (1896-1977) Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953), or Crosby and Danny Kaye in Curtiz's White Christmas (1954). Crosby teamed up with Sinatra and Grace Kelly in High Society (1956), a remake of The Philadelphia Story (1940).

In 1956, Elvis Presley made his film debut with Love Me Tender (1956). The musicals that followed were built around his sexualized, simple-hearted presence, but his potential was sabotaged by poor career management. Frank Tashlin's (1913-1972) The Girl Can't Help It (1956) was the first great pop musical, with appearances by attractive young artists such as Eddie Cochran (1938-1960), Little Richard and Fats Domino.

information.contentTitle: Scene from Porgy and Bess (1959) with Summertime
information.contentText: Porgy and Bess is based on the folk opera of the same name, with a libretto by DuBose Heyward and music by George Gershwin. The musical premiered on Broadway in October 1935 and has been revived regularly, always with enormous success. The score includes several classic George Gershwin songs, with lyrics by either his brother Ira or DuBose Heyward. Among them are "Summertime", "It Ain't Necessarily So", "I Got Plenty o' Nuttin'" and "I Loves You, Porgy".

content_list.content_text: But Richard Lester (b. 1932) would end up changing the game with A Hard Day's Night (1964). Using creative song montages instead of revered performances, Lester started a process through which the movie musical would eventually be replaced by music videos, turned into something secondary to a music career.

movies.title: Singin' in the Rain
movies.overview: In 1927 Hollywood, a silent film production company and cast make a difficult transition to sound.

movies.title: On the Town
movies.overview: Three sailors - Gabey, Chip and Ozzie - let loose on a 24-hour pass in New York and the Big Apple will never be the same! Gabey falls head over heels for "Miss Turnstiles of the Month" (he thinks she's a high society deb when she's really a 'cooch dancer at Coney Island); innocent Chip gets highjacked (literally) by a lady cab driver; and Ozzie becomes the object of interest of a gorgeous anthropologist who thinks he's the perfect example of a "prehistoric man". Wonderful music and terrific shots of New York at its best.

movies.title: A Star Is Born
movies.overview: A movie star helps a young singer/actress find fame, even as age and alcoholism send his own career into a downward spiral.

movies.title: Yankee Doodle Dandy
movies.overview: A film of the life of the renowned musical composer, playwright, actor, dancer and singer George M. Cohan.

movies.title: High Society
movies.overview: Childhood friends Tracy Lord and C.K. Dexter Haven got married and quickly divorced. Now Tracy is about to marry again, this time to a shrewd social-climbing businessman. C.K. still loves her. Spy magazine blackmails Tracy's family by threatening to reveal her playboy father's exploits if not allowed to cover the wedding.

movies.title: South Pacific
movies.overview: Can a girl from Little Rock find happiness with a mature French planter she got to know one enchanted evening away from the military hospital where she is a nurse? Or should she just wash that man out of her hair? Bloody Mary is the philosopher of the island and it's hard to believe she could be the mother of Liat who has captured the heart of Lt. Joseph Cable USMC. While waiting for action in the war in the South Pacific, sailors and nurses put on a musical comedy show. The war gets closer and the saga of Nellie Forbush and Emile de Becque becomes serious drama.

movies.title: West Side Story
movies.overview: A remake of the 1961 film about two youngsters from rival New York City gangs fall in love, but tensions between their respective friends build toward tragedy.

movies.title: Oklahoma!
movies.overview: This joyous celebration of frontier life combines tender romance and violent passion in the Oklahoma Territory of the 1900s with a timeless score filled with unforgettable songs. Rodgers and Hammerstein's hit Broadway musical.

content_list.subtitle: The events that shaped the world
content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1940 to 1959
content_list.description: Asian cinema gains even more prominence with the release of several masterpieces. Film noir emerges and musicals continue to shine on the big screen. The Western holds on to its reign as one of the most popular genres, and one of the most important movements in cinema takes place in France: the French New Wave.
